question: The Commission is assessing whether OpenAI’s ChatGPT should fall under the Digital Services Act (DSA) as a very large online platform or a very large online search engine. OpenAI reports that ChatGPT’s search feature alone reaches 120.4 million monthly users within the EU, almost three times the DSA threshold of 45 million.

This figure covers only the search function, which retrieves live information from the web, and excludes broader conversational use of the tool. The latest version, ChatGPT-5.1, exhibits a stronger ‘personality’, raising concerns about user dependency and emotional reliance.

Earlier models faced criticism for allowing children to create accounts without prior consent, exposing users to harmful content, and showing weak safety-completion mechanisms that could produce harmful outputs. Despite these concerns, OpenAI continues to release new versions without full transparency while making unverified claims about the mitigation of mental-health risks.
This raises three questions for the Commission: 1.

What is the timeline for determining ChatGPT’s designation as a very large online platform or a very large online search engine, and what interim risk-mitigation measures should OpenAI adopt during the assessment period?
How will designation criteria apply to a multifunctional AI tool like ChatGPT?
Could limiting designation to a single feature, such as search, create a regulatory gap leaving harmful features of ChatGPT’s core conversational function outside of DSA oversight?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Brando Benifei (S&D).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.2.2026) Pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 Digital Services Act (DSA),1 the Commission is to designate a service reaching, in the EU, an audience of 45 million average monthly active recipients (AMARs) or above as a very large online platform (VLOP) or very large online search engine (VLOSE). On 21 October 2025, OpenAI self-reported 120.

4 million AMARs in the EU of ChatGPT search.2 The designation procedure relies on a quantitative and qualitative assessment of the features of a service and involves consulting the national authorities and collecting views of the provider of the service under consideration, the absence of which would not however prevent a designation.

Without pre-empting the outcome of this process for ChatGPT, the Commission aims to conclude the procedure in the first quarter 2026. During that period, the service provider is bound by the due diligence obligations applicable to all online platforms. However, it may voluntarily comply with the obligations under Section 5 of Chapter III of the DSA3.

The DSA regulates intermediary services, and thus the assessment of the scope of a service is to determine which aspects thereof qualify as an intermediary service based on its integrated features,4 including on the characteristics and purpose of such integration5.

Providers of services falling within different categories due to the nature of such services are to comply with all the corresponding obligations,6 as well to risk-assess any new functionalities of VLOPs and VLOSEs prior to their deployment7.

Designation under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 is without prejudice to application of other EU instruments, such as Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (Digital Markets Act)8 and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act).9

3 Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065. 4 Article 3 (g),(i),(j),(p),(q) and Article 33 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065. 5 Article 3(i) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 states: ‘online platform’ means a hosting service that, at the request

of a recipient of the service, stores and disseminates information to the public, unless that activity is a minor and purely ancillary feature of another service or a minor functionality of the principal service and, for objective and technical reasons, cannot be used without that other service, and the integration of the feature or functionality into the other service is not a means to circumvent the applicability of this Regulation’.

6 Recital 41 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 states: ‘(…)To the extent that providers of intermediary services fall within a number of different categories in view of the nature of their services and their size, they should comply with all the corresponding obligations of this Regulation in relation to those services.(…)’. 7 Article 34(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065. 8 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj.
